extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, patent attorneys/agents, and USPTO examiners handling patent term extension (PTE) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining eligibility, calculating, processing, and issuing patent term extensions under 35 U.S.C. 156 and implementing regulations (including handling of due diligence, multiple applications, confidentiality, disclosures, and certificates of extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory agency determination of length of regulatory review period
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 156, the regulatory agency is responsible for the determination of the length of the regulatory review period for the approved product on which the application for patent term extension is based. The determination by the regulatory agency is made based on the application as well as the official regulatory agency records for the approved product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency publishes its determination in the Federal Register and forwards a letter to the Office containing total length and the relevant dates, separating the total into initial/testing phase and final approval phase. The agency's determination does not take into account the issue date of the patent nor does it exclude one-half of the testing phase. The Federal Register notice sets dates (e.g., 180 days after publication as a deadline for filing written comments or petitions regarding due diligence and 60 days for correcting published dates). The Office relies on the Secretary’s determination when calculating extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due diligence determination (definition and procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory agency determines under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(2)(B) whether the applicant for patent term extension acted with due diligence during the regulatory review proceedings. The term 'due diligence' is defined in 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(3) as 'that degree of attention, continuous directed effort, and timeliness as may reasonably be expected from, and are ordinarily exercised by, a person during a regulatory review period.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a due diligence petition is filed during the 180-day period after Federal Register publication, the agency resolves it and publishes the results; if no petition is filed, the agency may deem its determination final and notify the Office so the Office can proceed with its final eligibility determination. Regulatory review period determinations are not final until due diligence petitions and informal hearings, if any, have been resolved. A certificate may not issue until the determination is final unless an interim extension under 35 U.S.C.156(d)(5) appears warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation formula for period of extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Period of Extension = RRP - PGRRP - DD - ½ (TP - PGTP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: 'RRP' = total days in the regulatory review period; 'PGRRP' = days of RRP on and before patent issue date; 'DD' = days of RRP that applicant did not act with due diligence; 'TP' = testing phase period described in subsection (g) of 35 U.S.C.156; 'PGTP' = days of the TP on and before patent issue date. Half days are ignored for subtraction of ½ (TP - PGTP). The Office calculates length of extension using the regulatory agency (e.g., FDA) determination and the calculation is subject to statutory limitations (35 U.S.C.156(c)(3) and 156(g)(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not count review periods occurring before patent issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Any part of the regulatory review period which occurs before the patent was granted will not be counted toward patent term extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When calculating the extension, only the portion of the regulatory review period occurring after the patent issue date is considered. Half days are ignored in the arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction for periods lacking due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each period of the regulatory review period shall be reduced by any period determined under subsection (d)(2)(B) during which the applicant for the patent extension did not act with due diligence during such period of the regulatory review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periods the marketing applicant failed to exercise due diligence and thereby unnecessarily lengthened the regulatory review period after the patent issued are subtracted (DD term in formula). No determination of lack of due diligence was made unless so specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14-year limitation (35 U.S.C.156(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the period remaining in the term of a patent after the date of the approval of the approved product when added to the regulatory review period as revised exceeds fourteen years, the period of extension shall be reduced so that the total of both such periods does not exceed fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, the Office reduces the calculated extension so that patent expiration measured from approval does not exceed 14 years in total (example language provided in Notice of Final Determination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory maximums by issuance date and product type (5-, 3-, 2-year caps and variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations: (A) If the patent was issued after the date of enactment of the section, the period of extension determined on the basis of the regulatory review period may not exceed five years. (B–D) If the patent was issued before the date of enactment, various conditions lead to maximums of five years, two years, or (for new animal drugs/veterinary biological products) three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For products other than animal drugs/veterinary biologicals the calculated extension cannot exceed (A) reduction to meet 14-year cap, (B) five years (patent issued after enactment), (C) five years (patent issued before enactment but proceedings started after enactment), (D) two years (patent issued before enactment and proceedings started before enactment but approval after enactment). For animal drug/veterinary biological products similar structure applies, with the 'D' cap being three years. See specific date thresholds (e.g., Sept. 24, 1984; Nov. 16, 1988) and MPEP text for particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-specific calculation procedures and governing CFR sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure for calculating length of the patent term extension is set forth by product type in the CFR: human drugs/antibiotics/biologicals (37 CFR 1.775), food/color additives (37 CFR 1.776), medical devices (37 CFR 1.777), animal drug products (37 CFR 1.778), veterinary biological products (37 CFR 1.779).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The length of extension is the length of the regulatory review period as determined by the Secretary of HHS or USDA, but reduced where appropriate by time periods provided in the specific CFR sections. The Office will rely on the Secretary's determination of length of the regulatory review period when calculating the extension under these CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Final Determination — content and reconsideration window
rubrics_metrics.description: After reviewing information provided by the regulatory agency, if the Office determines the patent to be eligible, the Office calculates the length of extension and mails a Notice of Final Determination to applicant stating the length of extension and the calculations used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice provides a period (usually one month) in which the applicant can request reconsideration of any aspect of eligibility or the length of extension. Extensions of time under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not applicable to this reconsideration period. In the absence of a timely request, the Director will issue a certificate of extension, under seal, for the prescribed period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance, recording, and publication of certificate or order of extension
rubrics_metrics.description: If a determination under §1.750 finds eligibility and extension amount, a certificate of extension (under seal) or an order granting interim extension under 35 U.S.C.156(d)(5) will be issued to the applicant and recorded in the official patent file and considered part of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification of issuance is published in the Official Gazette; interim extension orders are published in both the Official Gazette and the Federal Register and identify the product under regulatory review. A file wrapper image of the certificate is added to the USPTO electronic file, and a courtesy copy is sent to the regulatory agency. No certificate/order will be issued if the term cannot be extended even if otherwise eligible; the final determination will so indicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No certificate if term cannot be extended
rubrics_metrics.description: No certificate or extension will be issued if the term of a patent cannot be extended, even though the patent is otherwise determined to be eligible for extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, the Notice of Final Determination will indicate that no certificate will issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret, confidential, and protective order material handling
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory or rule provision for withholding from the public any information submitted to the Office or the regulatory agency relating to a PTE application; proprietary or trade secret information should be submitted in accordance with MPEP §724.02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitted per procedures, the USPTO will waive the electronic filing requirement for that submission. Identification of proprietary/trade secret material should be made by page, line, and word as necessary. Such information will not be made public as part of the patent file before a certificate is issued. If the Office receives a FOIA request for the material, the applicant will be given notice and opportunity to substantiate the claim before the Office decides on disclosure. A petition to expunge filed before issuance may remove information; otherwise, information becomes public with the certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple applications for same regulatory review period — single-patent rule and priority rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In no event shall more than one patent be extended under subsection (e)(1) for the same regulatory review period for any product. Only one patent may be extended for a regulatory review period for any product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than one application for extension of the same patent is filed, the certificate, if appropriate, will be issued based upon the first filed application. If a single applicant files extensions for multiple patents based on the same regulatory review period and no election is made, the certificate will be issued for the patent having the earliest date of issuance. When multiple eligible applications exist, the PTE applicant will be given a period (usually one month) to elect the product or patent; failure to elect leads the Office to issue a certificate for a specified one. If applications by different applicants rely on the same regulatory review period, the certificate issues to the holder of the regulatory approval (marketing applicant), or to an applicant who holds express authorization from the marketing applicant. Applicants must inform the Office of various PTE applications per 37 CFR 1.740(a)(13) and 1.765; failure to supply requested holder information within a non-extendable period (not less than one month) is treated as establishing the applicant is not the holder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure (duty of candor) in patent term extension proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A duty of candor and good faith toward the USPTO and the Secretary (HHS or Agriculture) rests on the patent owner or its agent, on each attorney/agent representing the patent owner, and on every other individual substantively involved on behalf of the patent owner in a PTE proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals aware of material information adverse to entitlement to extension that has not been made of record must bring such information to the Office or Secretary as soon as practicable. 'Material' means there is a substantial likelihood the Office or Secretary would consider it important in determinations. Disclosures must be accompanied by copies of each written document and filed with the Office or Secretary (duplicate certified copies if material to both). Disclosures may be made through an attorney/agent or patent owner themselves. USPTO electronic filing system document description and code (e.g., 'Disclosure Under 37 CFR 1.765 in a Patent Term Extension Application', code TERM.PTE.DIS) should be used for USPTO filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of fraud, bad faith, or gross negligence (duty violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent will be determined eligible for extension and no extension will be issued if it is determined that fraud on the Office or the Secretary was practiced or attempted or the duty of disclosure was violated through bad faith or gross negligence in connection with the patent term extension proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If established by clear and convincing evidence that fraud was practiced or attempted or there was a duty-of-disclosure violation through bad faith or gross negligence, a final determination under §1.750 will be made that the patent is not eligible for extension. Since eligibility may be determined solely on representations in the application, final refusals on these bases are expected to be rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure when a terminal disclaimer is filed during PTE proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If a terminal disclaimer is filed during processing of a PTE application, any required updates to information already of record should be made pursuant to 37 CFR 1.765.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, if the calculation of term changes because the patent’s expiration date changes, an updated calculation should be submitted via the USPTO electronic filing system. Patent owners can use USPTO terminal disclaimer forms or file a self-prepared terminal disclaimer that meets 37 CFR 1.321 requirements. See MPEP §1490 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of third-party participation in PTE proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure pursuant to 37 CFR 1.765 rests on the individuals identified; submission on behalf of third parties, in the form of protests or otherwise, will not be considered by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any such unsolicited submissions by third parties will be returned or otherwise disposed of without consideration. PTE proceedings before the Office are ex parte matters between the patent owner or its agent and the Office; absent an invitation from the Director, third-party input is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express withdrawal of application for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for extension may be expressly withdrawn before a determination pursuant to §1.750 by filing a written declaration of withdrawal signed by the owner of record or its agent. An application may not be expressly withdrawn after the date permitted for reply to the final determination on the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An express withdrawal is effective when acknowledged in writing by the Office. Filing and acceptance of withdrawal do not entitle applicant to a refund of the filing fee. Except for withdrawals filed in response to a requirement for election, withdrawal after a determination must be submitted on or before the date permitted for reply and be accompanied by a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 with the appropriate petition fee.
